name: Coffee for skin / Cold brew

lead: Appearance communities promote coffee and cold brew, drunk or applied topically, for healthier-looking skin and looks in general.

Cold brew is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold or room-temperature water for about 4 to 24 hours and has lower titratable acidity than hot coffee. A 2017 umbrella review found coffee generally safe at usual intakes. The sources reviewed do not address skin, topical use, cellulite or under-eye effects of coffee.

paras: People drink coffee or cold brew daily, and some use coffee grounds or cold brew as a topical scrub or under-eye treatment. It is usually part of a wider skincare or diet routine.
Caffeine can cause anxiety or sleep disruption at high intakes, and pregnancy limits apply.

web.title: PubMed search results: topical caffeine and coffee for skin

angle.text: Appearance communities drink coffee and cold brew, or apply it topically, aiming for healthier-looking skin. Coffee has general safety and health research behind it; skin effects have not been studied in the sources reviewed.

lead: Coffee for skin refers to using coffee, including cold brew, to look better: drunk for its antioxidants and a perceived effect on skin aging, or applied as caffeine-containing creams, serums and coffee scrubs aimed at puffiness, dark circles and the look of cellulite [1][1].

Caffeine is increasingly used in cosmetics because it is biologically active and can penetrate the skin barrier; a 2013 review in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology describes topical formulations that typically contain about 3% caffeine [1]. Dermatology literature also discusses caffeine and coffee in sunscreens and other topicals [1].

Cold brew is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold or room-temperature water for roughly 4 to 24 hours and has lower titratable acidity than hot coffee [2]. Studies of its antioxidant extraction compared with hot brew exist [3]. On T Nation, cold brew comes up as an energy-drink alternative rather than as a skin product [4].
infobox: Skin aging, puffiness, dark circles, cellulite look

paras: Caffeine-containing creams, serums and gels are marketed for eye-area puffiness, skin firming and cellulite, and coffee-extract ingredients are used for antioxidant and anti-aging claims [1][1]. Researchers have also tested caffeine-loaded gels for cellulite using delivery aids such as sonophoresis [1].
Some people drink coffee for its polyphenols as part of a skin-aging or photoprotection routine; surveys and epidemiological analyses of coffee intake and skin condition exist [1].

Cold water extracts fewer of the acidic oils found in hot-brewed coffee, linked to lower acidity and astringency [2]. Caffeine extracts more slowly in cold water [2]. A 2023 review compares variables affecting antioxidant extraction in cold and hot brew coffee [3].

Coffee is associated with lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality and lower type 2 diabetes risk, with possible increased fracture risk in women and pregnancy concerns [5]. Unfiltered coffee can raise LDL cholesterol [5].

A 2013 review describes caffeine's mechanisms of action and cosmetic use, noting it penetrates the skin barrier and is typically formulated near 3% [1]. A 2022 clinical study of a coffee pulp supplement reported that after four weeks skin brightness, elasticity, spotting and collagen content were slightly better than baseline (p < 0.05) [1]. A 2024 Mendelian randomization analysis examined coffee and other beverages in relation to facial skin aging, and a 2015 cross-sectional survey looked at coffee and polyphenol intake and skin photoprotection in Japanese women [1]. A 2026 review in Antioxidants summarises coffee-derived materials as showing multifunctional value against skin aging, inflammation and barrier dysfunction [1].
No published trials of cold brew specifically for skin were located.
